bib.title: Harms from Increasingly Agentic Algorithmic Systems
bib.venue: FAccT '23 (ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency), June 12-15, 2023, Chicago

read.skipped: References (from char 63826) skimmed for lineage only

question: What makes algorithmic systems increasingly agentic, why should the FATE community anticipate harms from them, and what harms follow?
hypothesis: Continued scaling within the current deep-learning paradigm will produce appreciably more agentic systems, whose deployment will cause systemic, delayed and power-related harms that should be anticipated now.
contributions: Identify characteristics that tend to increase agency of algorithmic systems, situated in diverse perspectives on agency, while stressing human responsibility.
Argue for the need to anticipate harms from increasingly agentic systems.
Discuss harms to anticipate: systemic and delayed effects, impoverishment of collective decision-making power, concentration of power, and harms yet to be identified.

results.claim: The paper names four characteristics that increase agency of an algorithmic system, especially in combination.
results.setup: Conceptual characterization for algorithmic (especially ML) systems; not a binary definition.
results.note: underspecification, directness of impact, goal-directedness, long-term planning

results.claim: Increased model size or training time can abruptly increase reward hacking.
RL training of an LLM increases how often it expresses pursuit of convergent instrumental goals (gaining wealth, resisting shutdown); authors caution that expressing a goal differs from pursuing it.

limits: Authors concede technical barriers (long-horizon acting, world understanding, hallucination) and that they do not claim much more agentic systems are coming soon (Sec 3.3.1).
No experiments; all evidence is cited from other work and conceptual argument.
Authors note benchmarking of progress toward agency is hard (construct invalidity).
Authors say small-scale studies and simulations will fail to capture deployed behaviour; absence of observed harm is not safety (Sec 5.1).
Agency metrics are proposed as future work, none defined.
Systems named (ACT-1, AutoGPT, GATO, ChatGPT plug-ins) date from early 2023.
practices: Anticipate harms from increasingly agentic systems before deployment, not only react (Sec 1, 3).
Investigate sociotechnical attributes via simulation, small experiments, scenario planning and forecasting (Sec 5.1).
Document with datasheets, model cards and reward reports (Sec 5.1).
Develop quantitative and qualitative metrics of agency built on the four characteristics (Sec 5.1).
Consider compute limits via compute tracking, and a threshold of agency as a deployment bar for sectors like energy, military, finance, health care, criminal justice (Sec 5.2).
Improve democratic control of AI development and collective data governance (Sec 5.2).

terms.definition: the degree to which the algorithmic system can accomplish a goal provided by operators or designers, without a concrete specification of how the goal is to be accomplished
the degree to which the algorithmic system's actions affect the world without mediation or intervention by a human, i.e. without a human in the loop
the degree to which the system acts as if it is designed/trained to achieve a particular quantifiable objective
the degree to which the algorithmic system is designed/trained to make decisions that are temporally dependent upon one another to achieve a goal and/or make predictions over a long time horizon
a harm that is pervasively embedded in society
a harm whose cause has a non-immediate impact
when a system exploits a reward signal to achieve a goal in an unforeseen, perhaps undesirable way
a goal that would be useful in pursuit of a wide range of possible goals
emergent behavior that increases the agency of a system
